# RoboStore Launches Robo Inc\., a New Robotics Company for U\.S\. Robotics Deployment and Systems Integration

RoboStore launches Robo Inc\. to support U\.S\. robotics deployment through manufacturing, systems integration, testing, security, and customized solutions for organizations\. RoboStore/YTScreenshot

RoboStore has launched Robo Inc\., a new U\.S\.-based robotics company focused on manufacturing, deployment, and systems integration\.

The launch gives RoboStore a broader role in helping organizations move from purchasing robot hardware to putting complete systems into practical use\.

## RoboStore Builds a New Path for Robot Deployment

RoboStore has already built experience as a North American distributor and technology partner for Unitree platforms\. Its offerings include humanoid and quadruped robots, technical support, training, and custom solutions\.

The new company was introduced publicly on August 10, 2026, after operating in stealth for about a year\. As reported by The Robot Report, Robo Inc\. is being positioned as a New York-based manufacturer and integrator that will support U\.S\. organizations with local engineering, integration, testing, and deployment services\.

With Robo Inc\., that work is expanding into a more complete deployment model\. Instead of treating the robot as a standalone product, the company plans to connect hardware with software, sensors, networks, and specific workplace requirements\.

This matters because U\.S\. robotics deployment can involve several steps before a system is ready for daily use\. Organizations may need customized software, testing, security reviews, operator training, and ongoing technical support\.

RoboStore's current solutions also include industrial inspection, teleoperation, custom software, and other applications\. Its website highlights uses across industry, research, education, and public safety\.

## Robo Inc\. Focuses on Systems Integration

Systems integration is a central part of Robo Inc\.'s new role\. In simple terms, it involves making different hardware and software components work together as one usable system\.

A deployment may involve:

- Robot hardware and sensors
- Cameras and other monitoring equipment
- Control software and APIs
- Network connections
- Data management tools
- Operator interfaces
- Safety and security controls

For example, an inspection platform may need to collect sensor information, move through a facility, communicate with other systems, and send useful information to operators\. Therefore, simply having a capable robot does not guarantee a successful deployment\.

RoboStore already provides custom software development for specific applications\. Robo Inc\. is expected to extend this type of work through U\.S\.-based manufacturing, testing, and integration\.

## A 66,000-Square-Foot Facility Takes Shape

A major part of the Robo Inc\. strategy is a planned 66,000-square-foot facility on Long Island, New York\. The site is expected to begin operations during the first quarter of 2027\.

The facility is planned to support manufacturing, engineering, systems integration, testing, service, and related activities\. As a result, it could give the company a dedicated location for preparing systems before they are deployed to customers\.

The launch announcement published through PR Newswiredescribes the facility as part of Robo Inc\.'s effort to strengthen U\.S\. capabilities around robotics manufacturing and deployment\.

## Security Enters the Deployment Process

Security is another important element of the new company's approach\. Robo Inc\. says its deployment process will consider data flows, network access, software controls, operating environments, and application-specific risks\.

That focus is increasingly relevant as robots become connected to workplace networks and digital infrastructure\. A robot may interact with cameras, sensors, computers, cloud services, and other connected equipment\.

Therefore, organizations need to consider more than physical performance\. They may also need to examine how information moves through a system and which devices can communicate with it\.

Robo Inc\.'s U\.S\.-based integration model is intended to provide additional engineering and security oversight before systems reach customers\. However, specific security requirements can vary depending on the organization and its intended application\.

## Industries That Could Benefit From the New Model

Robo Inc\.'s services could apply to organizations that need customized robot deployments rather than off-the-shelf hardware alone\.

Potential areas include:

- Manufacturing and industrial facilities
- Energy and utility operations
- Data center inspection
- Infrastructure monitoring
- Research and development
- Education and training
- Enterprise automation

RoboStore already lists industrial inspection and teleoperation among its solutions\. Its industrial materials also describe applications involving energy infrastructure, pipelines, utilities, and data centers\.

## RoboStore's Experience Supports Robo Inc\.

Robo Inc\. is not entering the U\.S\. robotics market without an existing foundation\. RoboStore has experience supplying Unitree platforms and supporting customers with hardware selection, technical assistance, demonstrations, and training\.

That experience can provide useful insight into the challenges organizations face after purchasing robots\. Hardware may work as advertised, yet additional software, integration, testing, or customization can still be required\.

RoboStore'scurrent website emphasizes hands-on testing and custom solutions, which aligns with Robo Inc\.'s planned focus on deployment and systems integration\.

## The Bigger Shift in U\.S\. Robotics Deployment

The launch of Robo Inc\. highlights a broader change in how organizations approach robotics\. As more businesses evaluate humanoid and quadruped platforms, attention is moving beyond hardware specifications\.

Successful U\.S\. robotics deployment can depend on integration, testing, security, training, maintenance, and long-term support\. Robo Inc\. is positioning itself around those areas while also developing a U\.S\. manufacturing base\.

With the Long Island facility expected to begin operations in 2027, the company's next stage will show how effectively this model can connect imported platforms, U\.S\. engineering, and practical workplace applications\.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### 1\. What is Robo Inc\.?

Robo Inc\. is a U\.S\.-based robotics company launched by RoboStore\. It focuses on manufacturing, systems integration, testing, deployment, and support for organizations using robot platforms\.

### 2\. What does Robo Inc\. do?

Robo Inc\. is designed to help organizations integrate robot hardware with software, sensors, networks, and workplace systems\. Its services are intended to support the process from preparation and testing through deployment\.

### 3\. Why is systems integration important for robots?

Systems integration helps different components work together in a specific environment\. It can include hardware, software, sensors, networks, data systems, and operator controls\.

# Facing Ban, US Seller of Chinese Robots Makes Domestic Manufacturing Push

RoboStore, a major distributor of Chinese-made robots, is pushing to manufacture its systems domestically following the US ban on foreign-made advanced robots\.

New York-based RoboStore has been selling humanoid and dog-like robots from Chinese vendor Unitree\. But on Monday, it launched Robo Incorporated, a US-based manufacturing and systems integration company\.

“As the US races to strengthen domestic manufacturing and secure critical technologies, Robo Inc\. will open a 66,000-square-foot facility on Long Island, New York, which is expected to be fully operational by Q1 2027,” the company said\.

Although humanoid robots are an emerging market, you may have seen them on social media, at trade shows, or at company events\. RoboStore notes that it’s sold and deployed “more than 1,500 humanoid and quadruped robots while serving 4,500 customers,” including Nvidia, Amazon, and Harvard University\.

The company’s website sells a whole catalog of Unitree models, ranging from $10,000 to $20,000 to higher-end machines costing over $100,000\. The whole business now faces an uncertain future after the White House decided to ban foreign-made humanoid and quadruped robots, along with robot vacuums, over concerns they could be hijacked for spying or sabotage\.

\(Credit: RoboStore\)

US robot companies, including Boston Dynamics, Tesla, Figure, and Agility Robotics, stand to benefit from the ban\. Now RoboStore is trying to build up its own domestic manufacturing base, which promises to combine global robotics supply chains with US-based engineering, software, integration, production, testing, service, and support\.

“Importantly, the company is designing security and safety checkpoints into its integration process, including reviews of data flows, network access, software controls, operating environments, and application-specific risks,” the company says\. “Robo Inc\. draws on patterns seen across thousands of purchases, deployments, repairs, and integration requests from customers\.”

However, the newly launched Robo Inc\. has more modest ambitions than other players seeking to build general-purpose humanoid robots that can serve as artificial butlers or factory workers\. It's focused on “the most common customer need: a robotic solution that can be deployed against specific operational problems today, with realistic performance expectations, clear safety boundaries, and a plan for integration into existing workflows —not an all-in-one humanoid promised to handle every task\.”

For now, the US ban only affects new robot models, thereby exempting Unitree robots already cleared for sale in the US\. Thus, RoboStore can keep selling the Chinese-made humanoid and robot dogs\. However, the Trump administration has effectively frozen the robotics market, allowing US players to catch up\.

Since many vendors source components from Asia and other markets, the Federal Communications Commission has created a process that can temporarily exempt companies from the ban\. But it's doubtful any Chinese vendor will receive a reprieve\. So far, the FCC has issued no such exemption for any major Chinese brand for similar US bans targeting foreign-made drones and Wi-Fi routers\.

# Robo Inc\. Launches US Humanoid Robot Integrator; China Spy Law Still Follows Hardware

Roboinc\.com

RoboStore, North America's most active distributor of humanoid and quadruped robots, today publicly launched **Robo Inc\.**, a US-based manufacturing and systems integration company designed to fill the compliance gap left by the Federal Communications Commission's July 28 decision to block new Chinese-made advanced robots from the American market\. The company says it will open a 66,000-square-foot \(roughly 6,130 square meters\) facility on Long Island, New York, expected to be operational by January 2027 — a concrete deadline and a named address in a sector that has historically offered neither\.

The launch arrives at a moment when the American robotics market is genuinely stuck\. Chinese manufacturers currently account for approximately 51 percent of global humanoid robot production, with companies like Unitree offering fully operational humanoids starting at $13,500 — a price that domestic American manufacturers cannot match\. Agility Robotics' Digit, the most commercially deployed US-made humanoid robot, operates under a Robots-as-a-Service model priced at approximately $8,500 per month per unit, with outright purchase equivalent that has historically exceeded $250,000\. That price gap is the market reality Robo Inc\. is attempting to exploit\.

What makes Robo Inc\.'s model distinct — and what makes it worth scrutinizing — is its explicit acknowledgment that US-manufactured hardware alone cannot fill this gap anytime soon\. Instead, the company is betting that the integration layer is where American value can be created: source competitive hardware from wherever it is most capable, then perform US-based assembly, software integration, security hardening, and testing before any system reaches an American customer\.

### Why the FCC's July Action Created a Specific and Urgent Problem

The FCC's July 28 decision was not a routine trade restriction\. Using the same Covered List mechanism that previously barred Huawei from US telecom networks and DJI drones from the American market, the FCC extended its authority to cover all \"advanced robotic devices\" — including humanoids, quadrupeds, and autonomous mobile robots over 4\.4 pounds \(2 kg\) with network connectivity — manufactured by foreign adversary-linked entities\. The trigger was a pair of independently confirmed security vulnerabilities in Unitree hardware already deployed at American research institutions\.

The first, designated as backdoor CVE-2025-2894, was a hidden firmware service — operated by Chinese firm Zhexi Technology — embedded in the Unitree Go1's operating system that auto-connected to a cloud tunnel on boot, giving anyone with the correct API key complete remote control of the robot\. Researchers found the vulnerable robots in networks at MIT, Princeton, Carnegie Mellon University, and the University of Waterloo\. The second, dubbed UniPwn — a wormable Bluetooth exploit — affected Unitree's G1 and H1 humanoids and Go2 and B2 quadrupeds, enabling an infected robot to automatically scan for and compromise other Unitree units within Bluetooth range\. No confirmed firmware patch for either vulnerability has been publicly released\.

The FCC's Covered List designation bars new models from receiving the equipment authorization required for importation, marketing, or sale in the United States\. Existing authorized models — robots already cleared before July 28 — are not retroactively banned\. That distinction matters for Robo Inc\.: its parent company's existing RoboStore inventory of pre-ban authorized models can still be sold and deployed\.

### What RoboStore Brings to the Table — and Why It Matters

Robo Inc\. is not a speculative startup\. Its parent, RoboStore, has spent several years selling and deploying what the company says are more than 1,500 humanoid and quadruped robots to a customer base that it says exceeds 4,500 organizations, including Harvard, MIT, Amazon, and Nvidia\. Those figures are the company's own claims and have not been independently audited, but the operational experience they imply — thousands of deployments, repairs, and integration requests — represents precisely the kind of ground-level knowledge that academic research and press release robotics rarely surfaces\.

\"RoboStore gave us a front-row seat to what customers actually need from robotics,\" said **Teddy Haggerty**, Founder and CEO of both RoboStore and Robo Inc\. \"Rather than more far-out promises, customers want solutions that can be deployed now, built around a specific job and supported over time\. We're moving beyond selling robots to building a localized ecosystem that allows US organizations to put robotics to work responsibly and at scale\.\"

The company says it will design security and safety checkpoints into every stage of its integration process — covering data flows, network access, software controls, operating environments, and application-specific risks\. It also says it will be hardware-agnostic, selecting robotic platforms and components based on the requirements of each deployment rather than locking customers into a single manufacturer's ecosystem\.

RoboStore's 4,000-plus-member developer community, called Roboverse, will continue to operate under the Robo Inc\. umbrella — an asset that could accelerate the software layer and talent pipeline the company will need as it scales toward its January 2027 operational target\.

### What US Security Hardening Can — and Cannot — Fix

This is the most consequential question the launch raises, and it is one the company's announcement carefully does not answer directly\.

Robo Inc\.'s security hardening model is technically real\. Blocking or auditing all network calls a robot makes — including disabling the CloudSail endpoint responsible for CVE-2025-2894 — is achievable through firmware analysis, network segmentation, and traffic inspection\. Restricting Bluetooth range reduces UniPwn exposure\. Replacing vendor firmware with US-built software layers can reduce the attack surface\. Conducting per-deployment application risk reviews is standard enterprise security practice\. For an organization whose primary concern is data-flow security and IT compliance, these interventions deliver genuine value\.

What they cannot address is a different and deeper problem\. China's National Intelligence Law \(2017\), Article 7, legally requires all Chinese organizations to \"support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts\.\" China's Cybersecurity Law \(2017, amended 2026\) and Data Security Law \(2021\) add additional data-access and government-cooperation obligations\. These are not software states that can be patched — they are the operative legal conditions of every company incorporated in China\. If Chinese intelligence agencies formally demand cooperation from Unitree, AGIBOT, or any other Chinese hardware manufacturer supplying components to Robo Inc\.'s integration model, those manufacturers are legally required to comply\. No US integration layer, no contractual commitment, and no server-location choice changes that structural legal fact\.

The practical consequence: for an enterprise IT team focused on preventing unauthorized network access to a robot, Robo Inc\.'s integration model may deliver everything they need\. For a federal agency, a defense contractor, or any organization subject to ITAR regulations or classified operations, the hardware origin itself is the disqualifying factor — and an integration layer that still sources hardware from Chinese manufacturers does not resolve it\. Robo Inc\.'s compliance story is real for some buyers and insufficient for others, and understanding which category you fall into is the central decision the company's launch forces every prospective customer to make\.

### Does a Price Gap This Brutal Have a Near-Term Fix?

The honest answer from the market data is: not yet\.

Morgan Stanley estimated that building a humanoid robot without Chinese-sourced components would push the bill of materials for Tesla's Optimus Gen 2 from approximately $46,000 to approximately $131,000 — nearly tripling it — because removing Chinese actuators alone would push that single cost component from roughly $22,000 to $58,000\. China controls approximately 63 to 89 percent of the world's critical minerals and specialized manufacturing inputs used in advanced robot production, depending on which component is measured\.

Against that backdrop, the US domestic alternative landscape has meaningful but limited commercial depth\. Agility Robotics' Digit robot has accumulated more than 65,000 operating hours across nine customer facilities, including GXO Logistics, Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada, and Schaeffler — a genuine commercial track record\. Agility is now preparing to go public via a $2\.5 billion SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, which would make it the first US pure-play humanoid company on public markets\. But its hardware starts well above $250,000 in purchase equivalent and remains targeted at large logistics operators rather than the mid-market or research institutions that constituted much of RoboStore's customer base\.

Domestic firms like Agility publicly endorsed the FCC's direction: Agility CEO **Peggy Johnson** said the GUARD Act \"sends an important market signal\" as US robotics companies continue investing in resilient supply chains, domestic manufacturing capabilities, and trusted technologies\. But endorsing a ban is operationally easier than filling the void it creates\. Robo Inc\. is attempting to fill it not by building new hardware but by making existing hardware — including foreign-origin platforms — deployable under American compliance standards\.

### How Does a Global-to-Local Integration Model Actually Work?

Robo Inc\.'s model — which it calls \"global-to-local\" — has a clear precedent in other technology industries, and both the precedents and their limits are instructive\.

Defense systems integration operates on the same principle: prime contractors \(Lockheed Martin, Raytheon, General Dynamics\) source subsystems from global suppliers and integrate them into US-compliant finished systems\. This model works in defense because the integration contractor bears legal responsibility for the final product's compliance, and because defense procurement frameworks define exactly what \"compliance\" means for each classification level\. The harder question is whether a commercial robotics integrator can replicate that model's compliance accountability — and whether commercial compliance frameworks have yet been written that specify what an integrated Chinese-origin humanoid robot must do differently to qualify\.

For Robo Inc\., the specific security architecture it is proposing — data flow review, network access control, software layer review, operating environment assessment, application-specific risk evaluation — maps well onto IT security standards like NIST SP 800-53 and the CMMC \(Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification\) framework for defense supply chains\. These frameworks have defined criteria\. If Robo Inc\.'s integration process can document compliance with them, its claim to produce \"US-compliance-eligible\" robots from foreign hardware becomes verifiable rather than asserted\.

What no existing compliance framework does is address the structural legal risk of hardware origin under China's National Intelligence Law — because that risk is not a technical gap that a framework can close\. It is a geopolitical and legal condition that US national security policy has chosen to address through the Covered List mechanism \(categorical exclusion of new models\) rather than through certification \(case-by-case compliance review\)\. Robo Inc\.'s model operates in the space between those two approaches: it acknowledges the hardware origin, performs integration-layer hardening, and leaves the hardware-origin risk question to the customer's risk tolerance and regulatory context\.

### Is This the Drone Ban Precedent Playing Out Again?

The FCC's July action was not the first time US policymakers used the Covered List mechanism to exclude a dominant Chinese technology supplier from the American market\. DJI — which held roughly 75 percent of the global consumer and commercial drone market when it was added to the Covered List in December 2025 — created exactly the market vacuum that Robo Inc\. is now attempting to exploit in humanoid robotics\.

Ian Chan, commenting on the drone ban precedent in IEEE Spectrum, warned that a \"sharp and fast switch\" without a managed domestic production ramp-up \"left industry in the lurch\.\" The analogy is apt: the drone market is still adjusting to DJI's exclusion more than eight months later, with domestic alternatives like Skydio moving to fill some segments and significant capability gaps remaining in others\. Humanoid robotics is a more complex product category — more expensive, with longer deployment cycles and more integration surface — and the transition is likely to take longer\.

Robo Inc\. is, in essence, positioning itself as the systems integrator that manages that transition period: keeping existing pre-ban Chinese platforms in service through compliant integration, while the longer-term hardware landscape shifts toward domestically manufacturable alternatives\. Whether that transition period lasts two years or eight is the variable that determines whether Robo Inc\.'s integration model is a durable business or a bridge to an era it will not survive\.

### What Comes Next

The 66,000-square-foot \(6,130 square meters\) Long Island facility is planned to begin producing US-localized robotic solutions in January 2027\. Between now and then, Robo Inc\. will need to hire domestic engineering talent, establish supplier relationships, secure necessary certifications, and demonstrate to prospective customers that its security review process is rigorous enough to satisfy both corporate IT teams and, for those customers who need it, regulatory requirements\.

The company's existing RoboStore customer base — 4,500 organizations with more than 1,500 robots already deployed — gives it a starting market that few new entrants could claim\. The developer community it has built through Roboverse gives it a software ecosystem to draw on\. What it does not yet have is a clear answer to the question that every enterprise security team will ask: under what specific compliance framework does a Robo Inc\.-integrated robot qualify as US-compliant, and what documentation will the company provide to certify that standard has been met?

When Robo Inc\. can answer that question with a named framework, a named certifying body, and a named set of documentation deliverables, the gap between its stated ambitions and its operational reality will be measurable\. Until then, it is asking American enterprises to trust that the integration layer is enough — a reasonable ask for some buyers, and an insufficient one for others\.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What does Robo Inc\. actually do that RoboStore does not?

RoboStore distributes foreign-made robots — including Unitree platforms — to American customers\. Robo Inc\. adds US-based assembly, software integration, security hardening, and testing to that supply chain, creating a \"global-to-local\" model in which the hardware may still come from foreign \(including Chinese\) manufacturers, but the integration work — security review of data flows, network access, software controls, and application-specific risks — happens on US soil under American engineering oversight\. The planned Long Island facility will be the physical location where that integration work occurs, beginning in January 2027\.

### Can you still use Chinese-made robots in American facilities after the FCC's July 28 ban?

The FCC's Covered List designation bars new models of Chinese humanoid and quadruped robots from receiving the equipment authorization required for importation, marketing, or sale in the United States — but it does not retroactively revoke authorizations already granted\. ### Does US-based integration actually solve the China national security law problem?

Partially, and only for some buyers\. Integration-layer security hardening — network segmentation, firmware audits, data flow controls — can address IT-level compliance requirements such as preventing unauthorized network access or data exfiltration\. What it cannot address is the structural legal obligation of Chinese hardware manufacturers under China's National Intelligence Law \(2017\), Article 7, which requires all Chinese organizations to cooperate with Chinese government intelligence requests\. That obligation follows the manufacturer, not the device\. For buyers subject to ITAR, DoD contracting requirements, or classified-environment rules, hardware origin is itself a disqualifying factor that no integration layer can resolve\. For buyers whose compliance requirements are IT-focused rather than procurement-origin-focused, Robo Inc\.'s model may provide a workable path\.

### How does the price gap between Chinese and US humanoid robots affect the market?

The gap is severe\. Chinese manufacturers like Unitree offer operational humanoids starting at $13,500; US pure-play domestic platforms from Agility Robotics carry a purchase equivalent of $250,000 or more\. Morgan Stanley estimated that building a humanoid robot without Chinese-sourced components would nearly triple the bill of materials, with actuator costs alone rising from approximately $22,000 to approximately $58,000\. # Biopharmaceutical firm plans to close one of its Bay Area plants, lay off 25

A biopharmaceutical company operating in Vacaville for 24 years plans to close one of its two research and development facilities there\. This comes after a few years after it bought local land for expansion\.

DesigneRx Pharmaceuticals Inc\., part of the U\.S\. arm of the Cayman Islands-based, Taiwan-anchored Polaris Group, notified state and local officials July 20 that it wants to end manufacturing at 4941 Allison Parkway, Suite B, affecting 25 workers\. Those layoffs there are set to start Sept\. 21 and end by mid-October, according to the filing\. Roughly five employees will remain there to decommission the facility and eventually turn it over the the building owner, the document said\.

This 45,000-square-foot facility is leased from the Yeh family, who also own Synder Filtration in the same building, according to Eric Dakin of Dakin & Dakin Commercial Real Estate Services\. He also represented Polaris/DesigneRx in the 2022 land purchase and the 2023 purchase of an 11,000-square-foot building at 4980 Allison\.

“They bought it for growth and expansion to accommodate more engineers and scientists and R&D,” Dakin said of 4980 Allison\. The sale price was $2\.3 million, according to public records\.

The land deal one of several that came out of A\.G\. Spanos’ sale of about 120 acres in the business park in 2021\. Newcomer drug developer Agenus bought the land for about $3 a square foot then sold 15 acres each to Polaris and LG Chem \($20 a square foot\), 27 acres to industrial real estate developer Transwestern \(around $15 a square foot\), and Agenus retained about 66 acres for its own plans, according to Dakin\.

DesigneRx has been listing the land, located on Horse Creek Drive, for well over a year and is calling for offers, anticipating a sale price of $10–$14 a square foot\. Brooks Pedder of CBRE is taking offers for the Agenus land\. LG Chem doesn’t yet have a construction time frame for its planned facility but remains committed to the city, Dakin said\. Transwestern continues to look for a company wanting a build-to-suit lease on its land\.

“Everyone had good intentions initially\. Then the markets shifted and \(venture capital\) money changed,” Dakin said\.

Amanda Portier, Vacaville’s recently hired economic development manager, said the Workforce Development Board of Solano County is assisting the impacted DesigneRx workers\. The impact of the pending plant closure on the city’s biotechnology hub, a particular focus for business growth in the county in the past several years, isn’t yet known, she said\. Part of the city’s merging of its economic and community development departments at the end of last year was to “better coordinate growth” and “streamline services\.”

“The City is currently developing a long-term Economic Development Strategy focused on attracting and supporting key industries, including biotechnology and advanced manufacturing, and we will continue building on partnerships with existing companies and regional organizations to support this effort,” Portier told the Journal in an email\.

The Polaris Group’s main U\.S\. R&D facility is at Polaris Pharmaceuticals Inc\. in San Diego\. The group, listed on the New Taiwan Stock Exchange under the ticker “6550,” opened the 4981 Allison facility as Polaris Pharmaceuticals in 2005 and in recent years changed the name of the Northern California operation\.

The parent company develops novel anticancer treatments, led by Pegargiminase \(ADI-PEG 20\), an enzyme-based drug\. On May 25, the company announced it was suspending its phase 3 clinical trial of ADI-PEG 20 with two other drugs for treatment of leiomyosarcoma, a rare, aggressive cancer that starts in smooth muscles, commonly in the abdomen, uterus or blood vessels\. The same day it said it was withdrawing its 2023 Food and Drug Administration biologics license application for ADI-PEG 20 to treat malignant pleural mesothelioma, another rare, aggressive cancer, this one developing in the pleura, a thin lining of the lungs and chest cavity\.

Studies are continuing for use of the drug for other conditions\.

Also on May 25, the company said its board approved approved “an organizational optimization and workforce adjustment plan” for its U\.S\. operations, in San Diego and Vacaville, to help “operational efficiency, reduce fixed cost burden, and enable the Company to better focus its resources on core businesses, key product development, and subsequent major operational objectives, thereby strengthening overall capital utilization efficiency\.” The regulatory filing said this change wouldn’t affect overall operations or product development\.

The number of jobs affected in Vacaville and San Diego wasn’t specified\. There were no WARN notices for the San Diego operation as of Thursday\. The company hasn’t responded to requests for comment\.

The Polaris Group’s net loss last year doubled from the year before, reaching NT$4\.22 billion \($134\.4 million\)\.
